prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms brought the measurement of time to the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B015 as a single-part prize with Katori and Ye, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. Having read the full exchange, the chair's first question is the one that decides it for me, and I think the evidence settles it. The magic-wavelength condition is a distinct original idea: it cancels the differential light shift of the trapping field so that many neutral atoms can be held in a Doppler- and recoil-free lattice and interrogated at once. That is a different physical step from the 2005 comb prize (a counting tool for optical frequencies) and from the 2012 prize (control of single ions). The test I apply is whether the original experiment is identified and verified. Here the proposal and first strontium realization came first, and then agreement between independent laboratories at the 1e-18 level, with intercomparisons, has been reached by people other than the inventors. That is what makes me absolutely sure. On the credit division the chair asks about, I read the record as idea plus first realization for Katori, and the accuracy, stability and many-body clock regime that demonstrated the concept at its limit for Ye. I would not call Ye a later, more beautiful version of the same experiment, because that regime was not simply a refinement and is part of why the scheme is believed. The citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice and not only precision, so that it does not imply a single origin for the whole clock family, which meets Kroll's concern. On the redefinition of the second, I treat it as supporting evidence of maturity and not as a condition, because the prize is for the invention and its verified performance and not for a later administrative decision.
statement.case_against: The reservation that remains, and that I cannot remove, is novelty after 2005 and 2012. A reader who treats lattice clocks as the best next step in an already honoured field will call this incremental, and ion clocks (Al+) are a serious rival at similar uncertainty, so we cannot say that the lattice is the only route to this precision. The strongest fundamental-physics results so far are null bounds, as Kroll notes, so the claim that it reveals something new about nature rests on the capability (redshift across millimetres, many-body clocks) and not yet on a surprise. The redefinition of the second is still pending. Finally, the work of PTB, NIST, SYRTE, RIKEN and the junior people who built the clocks falls outside two names; I regard that as confirmation of reproducibility, but the citation wording must be careful.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube (B007) on a discovery-first principle, while saying openly that B015 is the safer choice and an invention in a field already prized in 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I take the discovery-first principle seriously, and it is close to the Nobel criterion that I quote myself: the original experiment, verified. IceCube is my second choice for exactly that reason. But the same criterion has to be applied to the names, and here B007 does not yet pass for me. You put Halzen, Karle and Spiering; I would credit Halzen and Karle; and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage and a collaboration of several hundred remain open. I am not yet absolutely sure about who did the original work, and that is for me a stronger reason to wait than the thin source population. If the committee could settle the names, I would be ready to put B007 forward in a later cycle, and I do not regard the clock as a lesser discovery: a lattice clock resolving gravitational redshift over millimetres shows something about nature that no earlier clock could.

responses.point: Kroll wants the citation worded so it does not imply a single origin for the clock family, and notes that the strongest fundamental-physics results from clocks are null bounds, while raising a two-part configuration with B057 or B007.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and I have put the magic-wavelength lattice of neutral atoms into the citation for that reason, so that PTB, NIST and SYRTE work on other lines is not displaced. On null results, I would say that a bound that tightens by orders of magnitude is a measurement result, and it is the kind of door-opening that I value, but I accept that it is not the discovery of a new phenomenon. On a two-part prize I remain unconvinced: B057 has no clean allocation among Pritchard, Chu, Borde, Kasevich and Mlynek and partly overlaps the 1997 prize, and B007 has the name problem above. A second part with an unsettled credit is worse than one part with a secure credit, and the three-person limit would also force Katori and Ye to share the configuration with names I cannot defend.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that B006 honours a secure single-particle flat-band prediction and the discovery of correlated states, and not a theory of pairing, and says he would not oppose a split.
responses.response: That distinction is helpful and it moves me a little: a citation limited to the flat band at the magic angle and the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states would not claim a mechanism. B006 is my third choice and I would support it as a fallback, which is why I list it as an alternative. What keeps me from putting it first is credit and timing: Yuan Cao, who carried out the 2018 experiments, is outside the three names, other groups reproduced the phases with variable samples, and I would be more comfortable after a few more years of independent measurements. I would put the question to you: can you say what a three-name B006 would do about Cao in the citation, as that is the original experiment that I would want to be able to name?

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, argues that B015 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and that the work of other clock laboratories confirms the result and does not mean missing co-laureates.
responses.response: I agree with the reading of the other laboratories as confirmation, and it is the same reading as mine on the 1e-18 intercomparisons. Where I add a caution is on the phrase that Katori proposed and Ye drove the performance: the citation should keep both as parts of the original work and not make Ye the author of a later improvement. I also note, as you do for B013, that I discount my own first-place ranking from the opening, since that subject lies in my field, and I do not ask the committee to carry it as an alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee finally accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I judge that it is, but a sceptical member can disagree without being wrong.
The exact weight of Katori's proposal and first strontium clock against Ye's accuracy and many-body record; I rely on memory and have not verified earlier lattice-clock proposals by other authors.
Whether B007 names can be settled (Halzen and Karle, or with Spiering) in a later cycle given the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage.
Whether the redefinition of the second, still pending, will make recognition of lattice clocks look timely or early in hindsight.
statement.conflict_note: I am a transmission electron microscopist at Chalmers, so the electron-optics ballot B013 lies in my own field; I discount my own opening first-place ranking, no longer propose it as an alternative, and would recuse from any decision on it. Göran Johansson, who works on superconducting circuits (B024), is a colleague in the Chalmers Physics department, which is a mild institutional connection that does not bear on my preferred configuration. I have no connection to Katori, Ye, or their laboratories, and none to the B007 or B006 candidates.
